reason: The sources contain over 10 cross-verified facts across multiple independent domain sources that bust common black hole myths with strongreceipts.
story: Despite Hollywood portraying black holes as cosmic vacuum cleaners swallowing everything in sight, gravity does not work that way. From a distance, a black hole's gravitational field is identical to any normal object of the same mass. If our Sun were suddenly replaced by a black hole with the exact same solar mass, Earth would not get sucked in. Instead, Earth would continue orbiting along its exact same path just as before. A solar-mass black hole would compress all that stellar material into an event horizon boundary only three kilometers wide. To get pulled inside, an object must cross this Schwarzschild radius, where escape speed equals the speed of light. Outside that boundary, matter falling inward heats up to millions of degrees and emits bright X-rays before crossing the point of no return. Black holes do not hunt down planets; they only trap what strays too close.
angle: If the Sun were suddenly replaced by a black hole of the exact same mass, Earth would not get sucked in and would keep orbiting normally.

claims.claim: If the Sun were replaced by a black hole of equal mass, Earth would continue orbiting along its normal path without being sucked in.
Black holes do not act as cosmic vacuum cleaners sucking in everything in their surroundings from far away.
Nothing, including light, can escape from inside a black hole's event horizon boundary once crossed.
The Schwarzschild radius defining a non-rotating black hole's boundary is calculated as R = 2GM/c^2.
A black hole with the mass of the Sun has a Schwarzschild radius of roughly 3 kilometers.
Stellar black holes typically form when massive stars collapse at the end of their life cycles during supernova explosions.
Matter falling toward a black hole forms an accretion disk that heats up and emits X-rays before crossing the event horizon.
Cygnus X-1 was the first widely accepted stellar black hole candidate identified in an X-ray binary star system.
Astronomers can calculate a black hole's mass by measuring its gravitational pull on nearby orbiting companion stars.
Supermassive black holes containing millions or billions of solar masses exist at the centers of most galaxies.
Supermassive black holes can accelerate infalling particles to launch relativistic jets near the speed of light along their rotation axes.
The early universe did not collapse into a black hole because space was expanding rapidly and lacked sharp density variations.
Pulsars were discovered in 1967 by Jocelyn Bell Burnell and Antony Hewish and were determined to be rapidly spinning neutron stars.
Merging black holes emit ripples in spacetime known as gravitational waves that can be directly detected on Earth.
Albert Einstein's theory of general relativity describes gravity as the curvature of spacetime caused by mass.

disputed: Cygnus X-1 stellar masses differ between sources: S1 lists 14.1 solar masses for the black hole and 19.2 for the companion star, while S2 lists 7 to 16 solar masses for the black hole and 30 for the supergiant companion; scripts should present these values as estimates.

The coining of the term 'black hole' is attributed to John Wheeler by some, but was used earlier by Robert Dicke, Life magazine, Science News, and Ann Ewing; scripts should avoid asserting a single creator.
